en: Om. Salutations to the venerable gurus;
salutations to the illustrious Sundaragaṇapati.
Re 32408 Notes:
• Words or letters within brackets are my suggestions (to the best of my understanding).
• Dots (... denote missing portions, leaf damage, or unidentified characters. • Each side generally contains five to six lines. • Notations such as (i.1), (i.2), etc., indicate the image number.
(2), (3), etc., denote the subsequent line numbers following the first *śrī mahāgaṇādhipataye namaḥ* (i.5b). May there be auspiciousness; may there be no obstacles.
We worship the elephant-faced one, the lotus-sun, who is day and night the elephant-faced;
we worship the one with many tusks, yet for his devotees he is the one-tusked.
The ritual procedure for the nine sacrificial pits (navakuṇḍa-pakṣa) is as follows: Homage to the one residing on the banks of the Kampa, [who is] the... of Kāmākṣī’s breasts!
Homage to you, the God of gods, the glorious Ekāmra...!
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇādhipati. May there be auspiciousness— may all be of the nature of Śiva.

In the nine-pit arrangement, according to the verse, one who has been consecrated while stationed in the eastern four-cornered pit should worship the fire named Āhavanīya; having performed the pacification with wheat, grain, and other offerings, and employing all mantras,
he should then sequentially cast the *kṣmāmūrti* [earth-form] and the *puruṣa* mantra into the nine pits.
In this [rite], the preceptor, acting as the officiant according to the prescribed rules, should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *Śivāstra* mantra.

(3) In the fire-pit known as the *yoni*, which is well-proportioned and shaped like a lotus, and while seated therein, (4) he should subsequently offer oblations of *vaṭa* wood, mustard seeds, and so forth, accompanied by the *Vṛddhāgni* [mantra]. (5)
For the sake of increasing progeny, one should perform the rite according to the rules in the form of Artha; then, having established the Southern Fire (Dakṣiṇāgni) in the form of Vahni,
which is formidable and beautiful in appearance, one should subsequently offer oblations with the *Hṛdayaja* and *Pratyaṅgirā* weapons in the south,
in a crescent-shaped fire-pit (*candrārdhakuṇḍa*), while seated upon a bed.
For the purpose of destroying the enemies of one's form, one should worship Khadira wood mixed with sesame seeds while kindling the fire in the middle;
and one should offer the Ghorāstra weapon, joined with the most excellent mantra of the Ghorā form of Śarva.
Thus, one whose nature is devotion should be firmly inspired by the excellent Guru. (2–3)

From the southwest, there is a triangle; in its center is a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) where the fire of youth is seated with the wife of Dhṛta as its own form, [fed] by sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the Plakṣa tree.
(4) And the form of Arka becomes Śānti; [one should worship] the form of the Great Lord of the Rule (Vidhi-Mahādeveśa) together with the wife of Dhṛta. (5)
One should sacrifice with the flame resulting from the oblation of wealth consisting of the *gāyatrī* mantra; it is offered by the preceptor. || 4 ||
In the western direction, within a circular space shaped like a bow and joined with the weapon of the sky (ākāśāstra),

for the purpose of Parjanya, one should offer oblations according to the rite using *samidh* wood, *pippala* fruits, and *mudga* beans. In the center, joined with the domestic fire (*gārhapatya*), one who possesses water recites the mantra while facing the form of Rudra, the Lord.
One should contemplate the mantra known as Sadyojāta, which follows that [mantra], within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

(2) In the northwest, in a six-cornered pit with its apex facing east, situated upon a human corpse and joined with the fire known as "the infant" (bālavahni), the preceptor performs the oblation in the center with *caṇaka* beans using a ladle made of *udumbara* wood. (3)
In the northwest, one should meditate upon the form [of the deity], the crest-jewel, the armor, and the increase of crops;

joined with the *sāvimantra* and following the prescribed rite, he becomes one who purifies. (6) In the northeast, in a lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), well-maintained and occupied by one seated in the form of a child—

In the midst of that, within the *kevalāgni* which bestows the fruit of complete victory, [the practitioner] should recite the *pāśupatāstra* mantra while standing beneath a *bilva* tree. Reciting the *vāmākhya* mantra of Paśupati upon that [fire], he becomes a showerer of nectar through the power of the intended meaning (*bhāvārthaśakti*), provided he is guided by a teacher using *āḍhaka* measures. || 7 ||
In the northeast corner, the personage situated there is equal to Puruṣa and endowed with the common qualities of Fire;
(2) he is fashioned from grains such as *māṣa* and others, along with a razor, and his form is called "Weapon-Space" (*astravyoma*).
(3) In this sacrifice of Īśa, the presiding deity of the image (*mūrtipa*) becomes the god Īśa, conjoined with the ritual procedure. (4)
The Guru, possessing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is honored by the crest of the excellent mantra. || 8 ||
A man situated between Indra and Īśāna, holding a circular sacrificial pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*), [should kindle] the Śiva-fire.

In that [fire], having offered oblations with wild rice (*nīvāra*) and bamboo sticks as fuel, he should offer a *palāśa* twig in the center. Then, [he should recite] the Weapon-mantra, the Īśāna-mantra, the Eye-mantra, and subsequently the Śiva-mantra, which bestows all accomplishments.
One who is intent on the goal of existence should meditate with even greater firmness upon the Lord of Pārvatī through the Guru.
(I.8b) The verse concerning the nine sacrificial pits is complete.

In the eastern [direction], in the square *tatpuruṣa* male-form *kuṇḍa*, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with the fourth foot, one should project the *mūrti* into one's own heart and [recite]: *oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtyadhipataye bhavāya namaḥ*. In the principal *kuṇḍa*, having visualized the fire in nine ways, [one offers] in the east:
*oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣamūrtaye namaḥ*.
A man resembling gold in hue, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread,
holding a citron and a rosary, and bearing the moon upon his crest.

Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. Having offered three oblations and having taken the fire in a shallow vessel (*śarāva*), one places it in the eastern square pit (*caturaśrakuṇḍa*), kindles it, and [offers]: Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Āhavanīya fire. Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the form of the Āhavanīya fire. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
He has one face and three eyes, three girdles, and three feet.
In his right hands, he holds a rosary, a trident, and a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*).

One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire in the center of the eastern sacrificial pit as being red in color, seated comfortably, and draped in yellow garments, holding a goad, a hand-drum, and a sacrificial ladle in his left hands. (3–4)

Having thus invoked [the deity], and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat-grass bundles (*viṣṭara*) in the girdles starting from the east for the protection of the fire, (5) having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having worshipped with the *saṃhitā*, [one offers] "Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to the seat of Tatpuruṣa. (Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to the form of Tatpuruṣa. (6) The meditation (*dhyāna*):
A man resembling gold, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread, holding a citron and a rosary, and bearing the moon upon his crest. (i.9b)

Having thus invoked and worshipped [the deity], and having performed the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire, [one recites]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣmāmūrti. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
He is remembered as having four faces and eight arms, wearing yellow garments;
he stands upon a tortoise, possesses a gentle form, is fragrant, and is surrounded by rivers. (2)

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kṣmāmūrti. Oṃ (3) hāṃ, salutation to Bhava, the lord of Kṣmāmūrti. Having thus performed the worship, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with: Oṃ heṃ hūṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the Āhavanīya fire. (4) Oṃ heṃ, to the face of Tatpuruṣa, huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Then the illumination (*dīpana*) with: Oṃ heṃ, to the face of Tatpuruṣa, huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ heṃ, to Tatpuruṣa, svāhā. Oṃ hūṃ, to the Āhavanīya fire, svāhā.

Having thus offered one hundred oblations for each, and having offered the Śivāstra-mantra, as well as the materials such as *śamī* fuel-sticks, rice, clarified butter, wheat, and so forth—along with the Śivāstra-mantra which bestows the fruit of all creation—one should meditate.

In the southern *kuṇḍa*, which is semi-circular in shape and represents the neuter (*napuṃsaka*) form, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps. Then, in one's own heart, one should worship and offer three oblations (*āhuti*) while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-mūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the presiding lord of the form of the sacrificer. Then, in the primary *kuṇṇḍa* to the south: "Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora. Having thus worshipped, one should offer three oblations. Taking the fire in a shallow dish (*śarāva-pātra*), placing it in the southern *kuṇḍa*, and kindling it, one should meditate while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire."
He has two faces, the luster of gold, three feet, and seven hands;
there are four tongues, beginning with Hiraṇyā, in his right face.
The three tongues beginning with Suprabhā are situated in the left face. (6) Śakti, Agni, and the *sruva* ladle are on the right, along with the vessel of clarified butter.
Having meditated upon [the deity] holding a trident and an axe in his left hands, accompanied by a goat as his vehicle,
and [bearing] the Dakṣiṇāgni fire in his right, one should worship him in the southern sacrificial pit.

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dakṣiṇāgni. Having thus invoked and worshipped [the fire], and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and grass seats (*viṣṭara*) on the east and other directions around the altar for the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, having worshipped the seat-form and the root-mantra with "Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to Aghora-hṛdaya," one should perform the visualization (*dhyāna*): "One should meditate upon Aghora, who holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a shield (*kheṭa*), a skull-cup, and a noose in his left hands, and an axe, a trident (*triśūla*), a sword, and a staff in his right;
he has a deformed face, is terrifying, and is adorned with serpents and other ornaments. (5)

Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the one whose form is non-terrible (Aghoramūrti). Having meditated thus and performed worship, one effects the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire, and [offers] Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sacrificer’s Form (Yajamānamūrti). The meditation:
Holding a black horn...
wearing a girdle of human bones, with limbs smeared with fresh butter, he possesses the beautiful form of the Sacrificer. (I.11a)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-mūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śarva, the presiding lord of the form of the sacrificer. Having thus worshipped, [one performs] the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with: Oṃ hūṃ hrūm, svāhā to Aghora and the Southern Fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*). Oṃ hūm, svāhā to the Heart of Aghora. [Then] the illumination (*dīpana*) with: Oṃ hum, huṃ phaṭ svāhā to the Heart of Aghora. [Finally,] having offered one hundred oblations (*homa*) for each with: Oṃ hum, svāhā to the Heart of Aghora; Oṃ hruṃ, svāhā to the Southern Fire.

(5) One should contemplate the collection of sacrificial materials—namely fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood, sesame seeds, cooked rice, and clarified butter—as well as the non-terrible weapon (*aghora-astra*), which causes the destruction of enemies.

In the northern lotus-pool (*padmakuṇḍa*), having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps, one should worship as follows: "Oṃ, obeisance to the moon-throne (*niśākarāsana*) in my own heart" (i.11b); "Obeisance to Paśupati, the lord of the form of the moon. In the northeast of the principal pool: "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the secret Vāmadeva. Having worshipped thus and offered three oblations (*āhuti*), one should take the fire in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), place it in the northern lotus-pool, worship it, and kindle it.
Then, having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra with "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the pure fire (*kevalāgni*)," one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Having two eyes and two arms, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
clothed in white garments, and possessed of white and red [complexions].

"Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kevalāgni. Having thus invoked and worshipped [the fire], and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seat-grass (*viṣṭara*) in the girdles starting from the east for the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), and worship them. Then, having worshipped the root-mantra of the form of the seat with "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāmadeva," one should meditate: [He is] red on the left, with a very ruddy luster, wearing a garland, garments, and a sacred thread;
he has a prominent nose and a reddish turban, and holds a sword and a shield in his hands.
Having thus invoked and worshipped, (3) and having performed the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of the lunar form*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
He stands upon a celestial chariot as serene as the moon, bestowing boons from his hand;
he resembles a jewel of universal form, holding a jar accompanied by the elements. (4)

Having meditated thus: (5) *oṃ hāṃ indumūrtaye namaḥ* | *oṃ hāṃ indumūrtyadhipataye paśupataye namaḥ* | having worshipped [thus], [one performs] the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with: *oṃ hīṃ hrīṃ vāmadevakevalāgnibhyām svāhā* | (6) *oṃ hīṃ vāmadevaguhyāya svāhā* | and the illumination (*dīpana*) with: *oṃ hīṃ vāmadevaguhyāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā* | Then, having offered one hundred oblations each for *oṃ hīṃ vāmadevāya svāhā* and *oṃ hīṃ kevalāgnaye svāhā*, as well as the *pāśupatāstra*.

Having offered oblations of materials such as *balis*, sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*anna*)—one *āḍhaka* in quantity—one should contemplate the increase of wealth.

In the west, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps (*catuṣpada*) in a circular pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a woman, one offers three oblations of clarified butter into the principal western pit while reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Water-form (*jalamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of the Water-form. Then, [reciting] "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sadyojāta-form," one offers three oblations of clarified butter into the principal western pit.
Having taken the fire in a shallow earthen vessel and placed it in the western pit, and having kindled it—[one recites]: *Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gārhapatya*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
With red limbs and adorned with red garments, joined in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
holding a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in his upper hands, he is decorated with ornaments of pearls. (I.13a)
He is endowed with seven tongues, has a single face, and wears matted locks.
One should meditate upon Gārhapatya mounted on a horse in the western fire-pit.

(2) Having thus meditated and worshipped, one should invoke him with: "Oṃ Hīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Gārhapatya. Then, for the protection of the fire, having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the grass seats (*viṣṭara*) in the girdles starting from the east, and having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should offer oblations into the center of the pit with: "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
He has white sacrificial ladles, is richly adorned with fragrant garments, has the appearance of a youth, and possesses three eyes.
[One should meditate on] Sadyojāta, who bears the moon and has hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

(5) Having meditated and worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta," (6) and having performed the union of the face of Śiva with the fire-face, [one worships] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the water-form. The meditation: "Having the nature of four arms, adorned with all ornaments... (i.13b).
Varuṇa, the bearer of the noose, was chosen as the aquatic vehicle by Makaraketana.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jalamūrti (2). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of Jalamūrti. *Ijyā*. Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta and Gārhapatya (3). Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the form of Sadyojāta. Thus is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Having offered [the oblation] one hundred times for each with "Sadyojātamūrtaye huṃ phaṭ svāhā" (4), and having offered the *vyomāstra* [mantra], one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks from the *aśvattha* tree and so forth, along with rice, clarified butter, molasses, and other substances (5), while visualizing the increase of crops.

In the southeast direction, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with the fourth step—in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a *pippala* tree and having the form of a woman; then, in one's own heart: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the embodiment of Fire (*vahnimūrti*). "Oṃ hāṃ, Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ugra, the lord of the embodiment of Fire. Having thus worshipped in the primary southeast pit, saying: "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Vṛddhāgni," and having offered three oblations (*āhuti*), one should take the fire in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), place it in the fire-pit, kindle it, and meditate while reciting: "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Vṛddhāgni."
Four-armed, three-eyed, with one face and wearing matted locks;
holding a trident and an axe, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
One should worship Vṛddhāgni, who has a white luster, is mounted upon a bull, and resides in the fire-pit (pāvaka).

(4) "Oṃ hāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to Vṛddhāgni. Having thus invoked the Fire-god, and having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the grass seats (viṣṭara) in the girdles starting from the east for the sake of protection, one should perform the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [one should worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Heart. The meditation (*dhyāna*) on the Heart is as follows:
the Heart resembles the moon and is endowed with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
I worship the one seated on a lotus, bearing the moon, facing Śiva.

(i.14b) *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Heart-form.* Having thus meditated, and having performed the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of Fire: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seat of the Fire-form.* Meditation:
The Consumer of Oblations (Fire), mounted upon a ram, with blazing eyes, holding a spear in his hand.
Shaped like a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), with its opening facing upward, blazing with the brilliance of fire.

(3) *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the form of Fire; *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to the fierce Lord of the form of Fire—[this is] the worship (*ijyā*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, *svāhā* to the Heart and the principal Fires—thus [performs] the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* to the Heart—thus [performs] the kindling (*dīpana*). *Oṃ hāṃ*, *svāhā* to the Heart. *Oṃ hūṃ*, *svāhā* to the principal Fire. Having thus offered one hundred oblations for each, as well as the *Pratyaṅgirā* weapon-mantra, and having offered fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the *nyagrodha* tree and others, along with materials such as rice, clarified butter, and mustard seeds.
There shall be an increase of progeny.

(i.15a) In the northeast, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four-footed rite—in an eight-cornered *puṃrūpa* fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should worship in one’s own heart: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Space-form (*vyomamūrti*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the lord of the Space-form. Having worshipped thus in the northeast of the principal pit with "Oṃ oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the Head," and having offered three oblations (*āhuti*), one should take the fire in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), place it in the northeast, kindle it, and [worship] with: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the seat of the common fire (*sāmānyāgni*)."
Dhyāna:

He bears in his right and left [hands] two faces, the Vedas as a horn, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a spear (*śakti*); [he also holds] a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and a spoon (*sruva*), the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a shield (*kheṭa*), and a garland. (5)
One should place the form of the common fire (*sāmānyāgni*) in the northeastern pit (*īśakuṇḍa*).

Having worshipped it with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the common fire," and having established the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) on the eastern girdles for the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration of the *sruva* and *sruc* ladles and clarified butter. Then, having meditated upon and worshipped [the fire] in the center of the pit with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the head," [one should contemplate] the mouth of Śiva and the mouth of the fire as resembling the color of a lotus and the sun, [and as] granting fearlessness and boons.
I worship [the Guru] seated in the lotus posture, bearing the crescent moon, and facing Śiva.
Having performed the *santhāna* (conjunction), [one should offer] *oṃ hāṃ vyomamūrtaye namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[He is] four-armed and four-faced, with a trident and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) in his hands.

Having meditated thus: "Holding a conch and a *khaṭvāṅga*, divine, with the luster of a jasmine flower, the moon, or snow," (5) one should worship with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Space-form (*vyomamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the Lord of the Space-form. (6) Having worshipped thus, [one performs]: "Oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the Head"; "Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the Head. The libation (*tarpaṇa*): "Oṃ hī(hīṃ), svāhā to the Head, huṃ phaṭ. This is the illumination (*dīpana*). "Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the Head"; libation. "Oṃ hīṃ hrūṃ, svāhā to the Common Fire (*sāmānyāgni*). Having offered one hundred oblations for each of these, as well as the *kṣurikā* weapon, (2).

Having offered oblations with sacrificial fuel such as *arka*, clarified butter, mung beans, and other substances, one should contemplate [the deity] as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation. In the southwest—in a triangular fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a woman—one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps. In one's own heart, one should worship: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sun-form (*arkamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Great God (*mahādeva*), the lord of the Sun-form. In the primary fire-pit—in the southwest—one should worship with: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Crest (*śikhā*). Thus having worshipped.

Having offered three oblations and having taken the fire in a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), one should place it in the *naiṛta* pit, kindle it, and [offer] "Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Yauvanāgni. The visualization: three-eyed, five-faced, red-bodied, and ten-armed.
In the right [hands] are a trident, an axe, a sword, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a vajra;
in the left [hands] are a chisel, a noose, a lotus, a wheel, and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*).
Hiraṇyā and Kanakā are on the right and left [of the central deity], while Īśā is at the top, with the remaining one at the bottom.
The wise practitioner should place Yauvanāgni, mounted upon a bull, in the southwest.

(4) Having thus meditated: "Oṃ hāṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Yauvanāgni. Having worshipped him in this manner, and having established the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and seats (*viṣṭara*) on the altars (*mekhalā*) starting from the east for the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), [he should worship] in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*): "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Śikhā.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

I worship the crest-lock of Śiva, rich with the color of vermilion, [displaying] the gestures of fearlessness, exposition, and granting boons; it bears the moon, stands upon its pedestal, and faces Śiva. (2) *Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the crest-lock.* Having thus meditated and worshipped, and having effected the union of the mouth of Śiva and the mouth of Fire, [one should say]: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sun-form.* (3)
Dhyāna—Ravi is mounted upon a horse, wearing armor and earrings, bearing a banner; he wears a crown, holds a lotus in his hand, and is adorned with an Aruṇa who serves as his charioteer. (4)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sun-form (arkamūrti). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahādeva, the lord of the Sun-form. (5) Having thus worshipped, [one performs the following]: Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock (śikhā) [of] Yauvanāgni. Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock. The libation (tarpaṇa): Oṃ hūṃ, vauṣaṭ svāhā to the crest-lock. Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to the crest-lock. Oṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Yauvanāgni. (2) Having thus offered one hundred oblations for each with the Śiva-Gāyatrī mantra, and...

Having offered oblations with sacrificial fuel such as *plakṣa*, with rice, clarified butter, and other substances such as [the *śalya*], one should contemplate [the fire] as bestowing peace. (3) In the northwest, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)—beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four steps—in a hexagonal male-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should worship]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāyu. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīma, the lord of the form of Vāyu. (5) In the primary sacrificial pit, in the quarter of Vāyu, having worshipped with "Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor (*kavaca*)," and having offered three oblations, one should take up the fire in a shallow dish (*śarāva*). (6)
Having placed [the fire] in the wind-pit and having ignited it: *oṃ hūṃ bālāgnaye namaḥ*. The visualization:
two-faced, single-hearted, four-eared, and two-nosed. (i.18a)
He is mounted upon a bull with four horns, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun.
In the right side [of the hand] are the *sṛksṛva* ladle, the rosary, and the spear; in the left are the javelin, the fan, and the vessel of clarified butter.

One should thus discipline the "child-fire" (*bālāgni*) within the wind-pit (*vāyukuṇḍaka*). Having worshipped it with: *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the form of the child-fire*, one should establish the protective seats upon the girdles starting from the east for the sake of protecting the fire. Then, having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), [one should worship] in the center of the pit with: *Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor*.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
I worship the one who wears armor resembling a horn, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness, who stands upon a lotus, who bears a moon upon his crown, and who faces toward Śiva.
"Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor. Having thus worshipped and joined the faces of Śiva and the fire, [one should worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the wind-form.
The meditation: four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and of great strength. (2)
His hand always holds a goad with a curved tip, and his gait is ever steady.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāyu. Oṃ (3) hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīma, the lord of the form of Vāyu. [Having worshipped] with *jya*. Oṃ haiṃ hūṃ, *kavacāya* huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ (4) haiṃ, *kavacāya* svāhā. Thus is the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Oṃ haiṃ *kavacāya* huṃ phaṭ svāhā—this is the illumination (*dīpana*). Oṃ haiṃ (5) *kavacāya* svāhā. Oṃ hūṃ, to the youthful fire (*bālāgni*) svāhā. Having thus offered one hundred oblations for each, as well as the Sāvitrī mantra.

(i.19a) Having offered oblations with *audumbara* fuel-sticks, rice, clarified butter, chickpeas, and other substances, one should visualize the increase of the harvest. Then, in the principal fire-pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*), for the purpose of averting [evil] from the place, averting [evil] from the time, and for the sake of averting both ill omens and auspicious signs, one should offer four hundred oblations with the root mantra. For the sake of purification, one should offer fifteen oblations with the root mantra. The pit in the east should be square; in the southeast, it should be shaped like a vulva (*bhagākṛti*); in the south, it should be a half-moon; and in the southwest, it should be triangular.
In the west, a circular pit; in the northwest, a hexagon;
(5) in the north, a lotus-shaped pit; and in the northeast, an octagon. Between Indra and Īśāna, one should cause a circular pit to be made. (i.19b)
O Brahmins, the quadrangular shape is the means for accomplishing all desires and goals;
it increases progeny and is the source [of prosperity]; the semicircular shape destroys enemies.
The triangular shape is declared to be for pacification, while the circular shape is for the sake of rain.
A pentagon is for the purpose of destroying diseases, and a lotus is for the sake of obtaining a wife.
(3) An octagon is known to bestow nourishment, and a hexagon increases crops.
Situated between Indra and Īśāna, it becomes the granter of all perfections. (4)
The eight-cornered, the four-cornered, and the circular—these are called the six-cornered;
[the square] is declared to be the "male" pit, or it is said that the pit may be situated [otherwise].
(5) The shape of a womb, the triangle, the circle, and the lotus-pit. (i.20a)
The female form is likewise described; it is called Āsīkuṇḍa.
The remainder should be known as neuter; the bed is called a *kuṇḍa*.
(2) Among the former [types], the *vṛddhā* sword is recommended for the Āhavanīya fire-corner.
In the south shall be the Dakṣiṇāgni; in the southwest, the Yauvanāgni.
In the west, the Gārhapatyāgni; and in the northwest, the Bālāgni. (3) The Kevalāgni shall be in the north, and the Sāmānyāgni in the northeast. (4)
In the primary [fire-pit], there should be fire like that of Śiva; then, following the sequence beginning from the east, there are Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, and the Moon.
These are the eight forms ending with Space, which bestow their own forms upon the sacrificial pits.

The embodiment of Earth (Kṣmāmūrti) is in the eastern quarter; the embodiment of Fire (Vahnimūrti) is in the southeast corner. In the south is the Sacrificer (Yajamāna), and likewise in the southwest is the Sun (Arka). In the west shall be the embodiment of Water (Jalamūrti), and in the northwest the embodiment of Wind (Vāyumūrti).
In the north is Niśākara, and in the northeast is Vyomamūrtipa;
Bhava, Ugra, Śarva, Mahādeva,
Rudraka, Bhīma, Paśupati, and Īśāna are the eight forms [of Śiva].
Bhava is in the eastern sacrificial pit, and Ugra is in the southeast;
Śarva is in the southern pit, while Mahādeva is in the southwest;
Rudra is in the western portion, and Bhīma is in the northwest.
Paśupati is in the northern pit, and Īśa is in the northeast;
Puruṣa is in the eastern pit, and Aghora is in the south;
Vāmadeva is in the north, and Sadyojāta is in the west.
One should place the Heart in the southeast, and likewise the Head in the [northeast];
the Tuft in the southwest, and the Armor in the northwest;
and both the Eye and the Weapon should be assigned to the Śiva-pit.
The *śamī* tree is indeed in the eastern direction, and likewise the *vaṭa* in the southeast;
the *khādira* is in the south, and the *plakṣa* in the region of the southwest.
(4) The *aśvattha* is in the western portion, and the *udumbara* is in the northwest. (5)
One should plant the bilva tree in the direction of Soma (the north) and the arka tree in the domain of Īśāna (the northeast).
Between Indra and Īśāna, one should offer a *palāśa* leaf in the fire of Śiva;
likewise, one should offer wheat in the eastern direction and mustard seeds in the southeast.
In the south, sesame seeds; in the southwest, rice grain; in the west, mung beans;
and in the northwest, chickpeas.

In a pleasant region, one *āḍhaka* [is the measure]; in the *īśakuṇḍaka* [region], it is indeed a *māṣa*. In a circular [field], there is bamboo and wild rice; in the *pradhānaka*, however, there is *niṣvāka*.
The fruit of the [first] day is supreme.
(3) But in the east there is an abundance of progeny; in the southeast, the acquisition of a daughter;
in the south, the destruction of enemies; and in the southwest, the eradication of disease. (4)

In the west there shall be an increase of crops; in the northeast, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Between Indra and Īśāna, it becomes the granter of all accomplishments. (5) This is the section on the five fire-pits (*pañcakuṇḍa*).

In the eastern square-shaped *kuṇḍa*, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and ending with the four-footed rite (*catuṣpada*), one should project the form (*mūrti*) into one's own heart. Having projected [it] with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāyu; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara, the lord of the form of Vāyu," one should divide the fire in the principal *kuṇḍa*... and, in the eastern direction, offer three oblations with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart, the face of Tatpuruṣa; svāhā."

Taking the fire from its place into a shallow vessel (*śarāva*), and having cast it into the square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the east, he kindles it. (4) *Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Āhavanīya fire.* The visualization (*dhyāna*):
one-faced and three-eyed, with three girdles and three feet. (5)
In his right hands, he holds a rosary, a trident, and a sacrificial ladle.
In his left hands he holds a goad, a hand-drum, and a bow;
he is red in color, seated comfortably, and draped in yellow garments.
One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire in the center of the eastern pit.

Having invoked it with "Oṃ Hūṃ, obeisance to the form of the Āhavanīya," and having worshipped it, one should arrange the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) on the eastern girdles for the protection of the fire. Then, having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having worshipped [the fire] with the *Saṃhitā*, one should recite: "Oṃ Heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

[One should visualize] a man resembling gold, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread, holding a rosary and a water-pot, and having the moon as his crest-jewel. (4) Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the form of Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart.
I worship the meditation— the heart, resembling the moon, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possessing a lotus and holding the nectar of the moon, facing toward Śiva. (5)

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Heart-form. Having thus invoked [the deity] and worshipped [him], one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire. "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Wind-form. The visualization:
four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and possessed of great strength. (2)
The deer-skin upper garment and the sacred thread, as well as the movement like a curling cloud.
Oṃ yūṃ, salutation to the form of Vāyu. Oṃ yūṃ, salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the form of Vāyu.
The visualization—in the eastern sacrificial pit:
three-eyed, with one white face, clad in a tiger skin, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
Resembling pure crystal, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
he holds in his right hands a rosary, a trident, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness;
and in his left hands, he holds an arrow, a water-pot, a lotus, and the gesture of granting boons.

Having meditated thus and performed worship: *Oṃ heṃ hāṃ tatpuruṣa-hṛdayāya āhavanīyāgnibhyāṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ heṃ hāṃ tatpuruṣa-hṛdayābhyāṃ svāhā*. The libation (*tarpaṇa*): *Oṃ heṃ hāṃ hūṃ tatpuruṣa-vaktrāya hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The illumination (*dīpana*): *Oṃ heṃ hāṃ tatpuruṣa-vaktrāya hṛdayāya svāhā*. Having offered one hundred oblations (*āhuti*) for each of these, and having offered the sacrificial materials of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), rice-grains (*anna*), and clarified butter (*ājya*).

In the southern *kuṇḍa*, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with the four steps (*catuṣpada*), one should project the form (*mūrti*) into one’s own heart, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the form of Fire (*vahnimūrtyadhipati*). Having thus projected [the deity], one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) at the location to the south of the principal *kuṇḍa*, saying: "Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ, svāhā to Aghora and Śiras. Then, taking the fire from that respective place into a shallow bowl (*śarāva*).
Having cast [the fire] into the southern hearth and kindled it, [one recites]: *oṃ hāṃ dakṣiṇāgnyāsanāya namaḥ*. The visualization:
[He is] two-faced, with the luster of gold, three-legged, and seven-armed.
And the square [seat] made of gold and other materials is on the tongue in the right face.
The three tongues, Suprabhā and the others, are situated in the left mouth;
Śakti and Agnisravā are in the right [mouth], along with a sacrificial ladle and a vessel of clarified butter.

Having meditated upon him as holding a spear and an axe in his left hands, and accompanied by a banner and a vehicle, and with the Dakṣiṇa fire in his right hand, one should worship him in the southern sacrificial pit.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. (Having worshipped thus with *iṣṭyā*), having arranged the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) upon the eastern and other girdles for the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as well as the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having worshipped [the fire] with the *saṃhitā* mantra: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
He holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a shield (*kheṭa*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and a noose (*pāśa*) in his left hands.
One should meditate upon Aghora, who is adorned with serpents and other ornaments, holding an axe, a trident, a sword, and a staff, and possessing a terrifying, distorted face.
Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the form of Aghora. Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Aghora. Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head.
I worship the one in meditation, whose head resembles molten gold, who bestows fearlessness and boons, seated in the lotus posture, with the moon upon his crest, facing Śiva. (2)

Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head. Having thus invoked and worshipped [the deity], and having performed the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire, [one says]: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Fire. The visualization:
The consumer of oblations (Hutāśana) is mounted upon a ram, blazing, and holding a spear in his hand.
The shape of the sacrificial pit, the face of the banner, and the blazing radiance of the fire.
Oṃ hāṃ (5) obeisance to Vahnimūrti. Oṃ hāṃ obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the Vahnimūrti.
Meditation—Rudra, whose body is smeared with ashes, [is to be visualized] in the southern sacrificial pit. (6)
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
possessing the luster of a ruby and encircled by a yellow garment;
he displays the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāna-mudrā*) in his right hand, while holding a book and a trident in his left.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, and having joined the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire, [one recites]: *oṃ hīṃ hūṃ hrūṃ aghoraśirase dakṣiṇāgnibhavāya svāhā*. *oṃ hūṃ hīṃ aghoraśirase svāhā*. The libation (*tarpaṇa*): *oṃ hūṃ hīṃ aghoraśirasābhyāṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The illumination (*dīpana*): *oṃ hūṃ hīṃ aghoraśirasābhyāṃ svāhā*. Having offered these individually, one offers oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), rice, and clarified butter (*ājya*).

In the northern *kuṇḍa*, having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), and having projected the form (*mūrti*) into one’s own heart—reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Water-form (*jalamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Earth-form (*jamūrti*); Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Water-form"—and having thus projected [the forms], one should offer three oblations into the principal *kuṇḍa* with: "Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva-śikhā. Then, taking the fire from that place in a shallow dish (*śarāva-pātra*), casting it into the northern *kuṇḍa*, and kindling it, one should recite: "Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Pure Fire (*kevalāgni*). The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Having two eyes and two arms, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
clad in white garments, and abiding in a state that is both white and red.
Having meditated upon him as being endowed with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne,
and consisting solely of fire, one should [visualize him] within the center of the sacrificial pit.

"Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the form of the absolute fire (kevalāgnimūrti). Having thus invoked and worshipped [it], one should arrange the enclosing sticks (paridhi), the seats (viṣṭara), and the coverings (paristaraṇa) upon the eastern and other girdles for the sake of the fire-lakṣa rite. Then, having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having worshipped with the *saṃhitā*, one says: "Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the seat of Vāmadeva.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[He is] red on the left, shining like a fine jewel, wearing a garland, garments, and a sacred thread.
With a prominent nose and a red turban, holding a sword and a shield in his hands.
(2) Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the form of Vāmadeva. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the seat of the crest-lock. The visualization:

I worship Śiva, who faces [the goddess], whose crest is rich with the color of vermilion, who bestows the boons of fearlessness and excellence, who sits in the lotus posture, and who bears the crescent moon. (3)

"Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Śikhāmūrti. Having thus invoked and worshipped [him], one effects the union between the face of Śiva and the face of Agni. "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jalamūrti. The meditation: His nature is four-armed, adorned with all ornaments.

Varuṇa, the bearer of the noose, is the lord of aquatic creatures; his vow is that of the god whose banner is the makara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Water-form. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the Water-form.
The meditation:
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu in the northern sacrificial pit;
he resembles the wind, has one face and two eyes, and is radiant with a crown and tiara.
Wearing yellow garments, bearing a conch, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with ornaments of pearls. (3)

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the water-form. Having thus worshipped and invoked [him]: Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Śikhā, and to the solitary fires. Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Śikhā. The libation (*tarpaṇa*): Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, huṃ phaṭ svāhā to Vāmadeva and Śikhā. The illumination (*dīpana*): Oṃ hīṃ hūṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva and Śikhā. Having thus offered an oblation for each, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), grain, and clarified butter (*ājya*).

(2) In the western pit—having performed the eighteen purificatory rites beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and ending with *catuṣpada*, and having projected the form (*mūrti*) into one’s own heart—one should project [the mantras]: (3) *oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kṣmāmūrtyadhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Having thus projected them, (4) in the western part of the principal pit, one should offer three oblations with: *oṃ hyaiṃ sadyojātakavacābhyāṃ svāhā*. (5) Having taken the fire from that place into a shallow vessel (*śarāva*), and having placed it in the western pit and kindled it, one should say: *oṃ hīṃ gārhapatyāsanāya namaḥ*. (i.28a)
Dhyāna:
[He is] red-limbed, richly endowed with a red complexion, joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
his upper hands hold a sacrificial ladle and a spoon, and he is adorned with ornaments of pearls. (2)
One should meditate upon Gārhapatya in the western fire-pit as being endowed with seven tongues, having one face, and wearing matted hair, mounted upon a horse.

(3) Thus [is the worship] of Jyeṣṭhā. For the protection of the fire, having spread *sudarbha* grass upon the eastern girdle (*mekhalā*), and having worshipped the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*), one should perform the consecration of the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, having worshipped the seat, the form, and the root-mantra with: "Oṃ hīṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta and Kavaca," (5) [one proceeds].
Meditation:
[One should visualize] the form of a youth, three-eyed, richly adorned with white unguents and fragrant pastes;
Sadyojāta, bearing the moon, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (I.28b)
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Sadyojāta form. Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the armor (*kavaca*).
Meditation:
(2) The armor is like a bumblebee, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
I worship the one seated upon a lotus, wearing a moon-diadem, facing Śiva.
Oṃ haiṃ, salutation to the Form of the Armor (Kavacamūrti). [I] worship. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Form of the Earth (Kṣmāmūrti). Meditation:
Having four faces and eight arms, wearing yellow garments, and holding an arrow. (4)
Seated upon a tortoise, of gentle form, and possessing the luster of a fragrant river;
[I bow] to Brahmā, the lord of the earth-form, obeisance.
Meditation—(5).
In the western fire-pit, one should worship Brahmā, adorned with a girdle of muñja grass and darbha blades;
he has four arms and four faces, each face having three eyes,
a yellow complexion, a beautiful countenance, and is endowed with variegated garments.
Complete in all its limbs, [carrying] a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot.

Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire. *Oṃ haṃ haiṃ hrūṃ sadyojātakavacagārhapatyāgnyā svāhā.* *Oṃ haṃ haiṃ sadyojātakavacābhyāṃ svāhā.* The libation (*tarpaṇa*): *Oṃ haṃ hai sadyojātakavacāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.* The illumination (*dīpana*): *Oṃ haṃ haiṃ sadyojātakavacāya svāhā.* Having offered these oblations (*āhuti*) individually, and having offered oblations of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), food, and clarified butter (*ājya*), [it is stated] in the *Vātula*:
Hereafter, I shall explain what is called the system of five sections:
(i.29b) The Āhavanīya fire is in the east, while the Dakṣiṇa fire is in the south;
the Gārhapatya fire is in the west, and the Kevala fire is in the north. (2)
In the northeast, however, is the fire of Śiva; these are proclaimed as the five fires.
In the central [direction], there should be the form of Earth, and in the east, the form of Wind.
(3) In the south, there should be the form of Fire, while in the north, there is the form of Water.
One should worship Kṣmāmūrti in the western pit; these are the bearers of the forms of the pits.
(4) Next, I shall describe the Lords of the Forms—from Pradhāna to the end of the west—(5) as follows:
One should install Sadāśiva as Īśa, and Īśvara preceded by *pra-*; Rudra is said to be in the south, and Viṣṇu in the north;
and Brahmā in the western part—in this manner, one should place the lords of the forms.

In the east, the Puruṣa-heart is said to be located; likewise, the Ghora-head is in the south. The two nooses are in the south and the armor is in the north; likewise, the solar [mantra] is in the southern crest.
The Eye and the Weapon belong to the Lord Īśāna; these are to be worshipped in the primary sacrificial pit.
One should offer oblations in five sacrificial pits using wood from the *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *udumbara* trees,
as well as wheat, sesame, and one *āḍhaka* of mung beans,
along with *niṣpāva* and bamboo seeds.

The fruit of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)—(5)—the sacrificial pit bestows the fruits of one's desires; the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) bestow the attainment of the knowledge of those [fruits]; liberation is attained through the sacrificial seat (*viṣṭara*); and by spreading the *darbha* grass around, the fruit of one's cherished goals is granted.
One should offer the *vṛddhi* oblation, which yields the fruit of prosperity and nourishment from clarified butter; the vessel (*pātra*) bestows victory and wealth;
the fuel-stick (*samidh*) grants liberation from sin; and the two types of sacrificial wood (*samidha*) bestow divinity and peace.
One should offer the *caru* oblation to destroy disturbances in the kingdom, and one should offer parched grain (*lāja*) for the sake of enjoyment.
It bestows sovereignty, fortune, happiness, fame, and auspiciousness; it grants sons and provides enjoyments.
One should offer oblations of grain to obtain a daughter, to secure victory, and to attain the status of a lord of wealth; this bestows success.
Milk grants the fruit of happiness, while curd, honey, and ghee bestow beauty and splendor.
(4) *Apūpaka* cakes made from flour and other ingredients grant fruits such as the destruction of disease, suffering, and evil.

(5) Betel (*tāmbūla*) bestows the fruits of fortune, fame, and enjoyment, and grants the accomplishment of all aims. Incense (*dhūpa*), when offered on every step with flames, ashes, and so forth, brings liberation from sin.

The fire bestows all blessings and is the state of Śiva; it is the full oblation of union (*sāyujya*). (6) In the fire, the fuel bestows the fruit of health, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) destroys disease. (i.31a)
There shall be an abundance of excellent grain, as well as good fortune and parched grain.
With mustard seeds one attains the destruction of disease, and likewise with barley, the subjugation of kings;
through sesame one obtains nourishment, and with mung beans, the increase of longevity.
It brings cattle, prosperity, and beans, as well as fruit and even unhappiness;
it destroys your enemies and bestows upon you fortune and indeed a cluster of virtues.
The coconut grants all success; the cake increases one's progeny;
and betel-leaf grants all success—these are the givers of fruits.
Having offered nine kinds of new grain, one should avoid the affliction of the planets;
having offered various foods in many ways, it bestows the auspicious increase of sovereignty.
There shall be cakes, milk-rice, and various kinds of edible foods;
having offered these into the fire, one obtains the fruit [of the rite], free from the fear of untimely death.
One should offer as oblation the fragrant substances of cardamom, cloves, and jasmine;
having offered them in many ways, it bestows the auspicious increase of the kingdom.
Having offered curd mixed with milk, accompanied by a red cloth, into the fire, one shall attain union with Śiva; thus it is stated in the Vātula [Tantra].
[One should offer] wood from the Śamī, Jaṭī, Khadira, Plakṣa, Aśvattha, Udumbara, Bilva, Arka, and [other trees].
Palāśa, apāmārga, panasa, āmra, dūrvā, as well as bamboo and beautiful pāṭalī;
clarified butter, caru, and well-prepared parched grain and mung beans;
niṣpāva, mudga, sesame, mustard, and rice. (4–5)
Barley, guggulu resin, *kila*, *ustha*, peas, wheat, *kāśa* grass, *kuśa* grass, *āḍhaka* leaves and flowers;

rice, barley, chickpeas, *cocaka*, *cañcā*, *kanda*, milk, curd, honey, molasses, sugar-cane, and candied sugar; mango fruit, plantain, jackfruit, sugar, grapes, *āṣkulika*, wood-apple, and *sallica*. (I.32a)
Milk-rice, sesame-rice, rice with ghee, curd-rice, and rice with green gram;
black-gram porridge, fresh milk-pudding, honey, clarified butter, and thereafter very pure food;
thereafter, according to the ritual procedure, tamarind, mustard-seed-rice, kālāṅgula, and sandalwood.
One should offer oblations of moon, sun, and lotus, along with sugar, honey, and clarified butter;
as well as dates, parched grain, cakes, darkness-removing incense, and thick cakes.
Milk and sesame produced from sugar-candy, which are pure, thick, and charming with their various corners;
*srīvera*, snow-water, musk, *kastūrī*, and *gorocanā*;
as well as *jātī*, camphor, cloves, *kumuda*, nutmeg, and fragrant betel-leaf. (i.32b)
Skanda and Kaurī [beheld] Maheśvara mounted upon his bull-vehicle.
Then, with offerings of flowers and unguents born of the essence of dharma,
he worshipped that [image] which had been fashioned by Viśvakarman with supreme devotion.
It held an axe and a deer in its right and left hands respectively.
With a hand granting fearlessness and adorned with a crown of matted locks, (3) bearing a mass of matted hair like Skanda’s, and decorated with all ornaments;
his left foot rests upon a corpse while his right foot is extended. (4)
Wearing a waist-thread tied below [the navel] and adorned with bracelets and other ornaments; with a leaf-shaped earring on the left ear and a crocodile-shaped earring on the right;
seated upon a lotus pedestal with his consort Gaurī. (5)

Having meditated thus in one’s mind upon the Supreme Lord known as Somāskanda-Naṭeśa— who is accompanied by Skanda and Śālāpūpa, and who grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims— one should worship Tyāgarāja. (i.33a)
In the case of sprinkling, there are fifty thousand; in the case of sight, eight [thousand];
in the case of binding with eight [mantras], there should be one hundred thousand; and for the restoration of the dilapidated, one hundred thousand.
Regarding the arrangement of the seats and so forth, three hundred thousand [recitations] are prescribed here;
for the goddesses beginning with Galā, [the rite is performed] with oblations of substances together with the mantras.
The Guru should offer one thousand and fifty oblations;
for the installation of Bāṇaliṅgas intended for oneself, the most excellent Guru should perform ten thousand oblations for the deities beginning with Soma and Skanda.
One should perform five thousand oblations, or otherwise offer one thousand;

for a pacifying oblation (*śāntihoma*), one thousand, but for a site-consecration oblation (*vāstuhome*), three hundred. For a general oblation (*homa*), it should be two hundred, and for a ritual bathing (*snapana*), it shall be one hundred.
In the performance of the daily fire-ritual (agnikārya), there is the offering of five hundred oblations; [the rest] is according to the scripture...

(i.34b *Navakuṇḍavidhi*) Now, the procedure for the Īśāna-kuṇḍa is described: The presiding priest (*mūrtipa*), having sat facing east on the western side of the eight-cornered *puruṣa*-shaped kuṇḍa in the Īśāna direction, performs the eighteen consecrations (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the inspection of the kuṇḍa. Then the Guru, having taken the fire from the Īśāna portion of the principal kuṇḍa into a shallow dish (*śarāva-pātra*) and having placed it into the Īśāna-kuṇḍa, the presiding priests kindle the fire.

For the purpose of preparing the fire, having strewn *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the northeast upon the eastern and other girdles (*mekhalā*) using the *astreṇa* mantra, and having likewise placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them, one should worship as follows: on the enclosing sticks—in the east, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā"; in the west, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu"; in the south, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra"; in the north, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] on the seats from the east to the northeast: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra."

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama. (2) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nairṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna. (3) To the south of that: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā. To the north of Nairṛti: Oṃ hāṃ, Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu. Having offered the *arghya* water, (4) having made a request for the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*).

Having placed the clarified butter—which has undergone the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) performed by the Guru—into a shallow dish (*śarāva*) from the Guru’s hand, and having taken it, he holds it at the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having placed two *darbha* blades, joined at their tips and tied with a central knot, into the midst of the ghee while reciting the *praṇava*, and having consecrated it with the mantras of Īśāna, Netra, and Śiras; having protected it and veiled it, and having rendered it nectarine (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the *dhenumudrā* while reciting the Root Mantra, he worships it.
And that [deity] is the Jewel-Body, three-eyed, endowed with the weapons and arms of Śiva.
Having meditated thus: "O Agni, since you are the sovereign splendor and the supreme purifier, therefore, having established [the deity] within the lotus of your heart, I offer libations."

Having thus requested permission from the Fire-god (*agni*), and having entered the body [of the deity] through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), one should worship the seat within his heart-lotus as follows: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairājñā(ya)ya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the seat, one worships that which is upon it: *oṃ hāṃ īśānaśivāsanāya namaḥ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*): [He is] crystal-like in luster, possessing three eyes, and bearing the moon upon his crest.
[One should meditate on] the gentle, serene Īśāna, who holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness.
(I.36a, 1) In the northeast, within an octagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the wise one should worship Īśāna.

Having thus meditated, [one should recite]: *oṃ hoṃ īśānamūrtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hoṃ īśānaśivāya namaḥ*. Having offered the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water of honor (*arghya*), and having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flower garlands, and so forth, one should worship Him with His mantra and display the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*). (4) In the northern portion of Īśāna: *oṃ hauṃ netraśivāsanāya namaḥ*.
Meditation—
[one should contemplate] the eye of the Lord as having the luster of the dawn, consisting of vision and action,
having the nature of the three principles (*tritattva*), and resting upon the triad of mandalas beginning with fire. (5)
[The deity] has a face beginning with ghee, holds [objects] such as a vessel in his hands, has one face, and has a trident in his hand; he is consecrated by Yogaśiva. (I.36b)

One should perform the Netra-mantra on the northern part of Īśāna. Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the eyes, the form of Śiva*; (2) *Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes, to Śiva*. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*), and having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth, one should worship with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra and display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*). (4) On the northern part of the Eye: *Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the seat of the head of Śiva*. The meditation (*dhyāna*):
His head, resembling refined gold, is wrapped in a yellow cloth;
he sits upon a lotus throne and wears a crown of matted hair with the moon at its center. (5)
Three-eyed and four-armed, adorned with all ornaments,
facing Śiva, she holds a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

One should worship the *śiromantra* on the northern part of the eye. (2) Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the head, the form of Śiva; Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the head, to Śiva," one should worship [it] with all the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with the invocation (3). Adorning it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship it with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra and display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*). (4) Then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so on, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire. (5)

Having offered one hundred oblations for each with their respective root-mantras for the purpose of satiating the mantras; then, for the sake of averting ill-omens related to place, time, and so forth, and for the attainment of auspicious signs, having offered four hundred oblations for each with their respective root-mantras along with the *pūrṇā* offering; and having offered one hundred oblations for each with their respective root-mantras as an ancillary part of the ritual of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*); and having presented the *pūrṇā* offering: *oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā*. *oṃ hauṃ netrebhyaḥ svāhā*.

Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the head. Thus is the libation (tarpaṇa). (4) Oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ, huṃ phaṭ to Īśāna. With these three oblations (āhuti), one performs the kindling (dīpana). Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ hūṃ, huṃ phaṭ to the head. With these three oblations, one should perform the kindling. Then, having offered a hundred oblations with *bilva* fuel-sticks using the mantra "Oṃ hoṃ, svāhā to Īśāna-Śiva," and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer oblations with *kuluttha* and other sacrificial substances as before, either according to the prescribed number or according to one's capacity. (i.38a)

Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā | (2) Oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā | Having thus offered four oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras at the end of each substance, and having given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), then (3) having first offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) to the Guru, and having given water for rinsing the mouth, betel, and so forth, and having performed recitation (*japa*), presented the offering, and paid homage—thus ends the ritual procedure for worship and oblation in the Īśāna fire-pit.

(i.38b *pūrvakuṇḍavidhi*) Now, the procedure for the eastern fire-pit (*pūrvakuṇḍa*) is described: the presiding priest (*mūrtipa*), assuming the form of Puruṣa, sits facing north on the southern side of the triangular or quadrangular pit. Having performed the eighteen consecrations (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the [rite at] the crossroads, the Guru takes the fire from the eastern part of the principal pit into a shallow dish (*śarāva*) and inspects it in the eastern pit.

The presiding priest (mūrtipa), having kindled the fire, shall strew darbha grass with their tips pointing northeast upon the eastern girdle for the protection of the sacrificial fire, using the Astra mantra. Having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and the ritual seats (viṣṭara) upon them, he shall worship those enclosing sticks as follows: on the east—*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; on the west—*oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; on the south—*oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the north—*oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus he worships.

(2) On the seats—from the east to the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*; *oṃ* (3) *hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vāyave namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. (4) To the south of that: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. To the north of the southwest: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped them and offered the *arghya*, (5) [one should proceed].

Having requested [permission] for the purpose of protecting the fire, and having performed the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should take the clarified butter (*ājya*)—which has been consecrated in the primary sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)—from the hand of the Guru using a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), and place it in the center of the pit. Then, having fashioned a *darbha*-grass ring (*guṇa*) one span long, with two tips and a double knot in the middle, and having placed it into the midst of the clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*, one should consecrate it with the two mantras of Tatpuruṣa and Astra.

Having protected [the offering] and veiled it with the root mantra, having rendered it nectar through the *dhenumudrā*, and having worshipped it—having thus meditated upon the Fire-god as possessing a body of jewels, three eyes, and arms endowed with the weapons of Śiva—one should place him within the lotus-heart of that [Fire], saying: "O Fire, you are the purifying supreme splendor of Īśvara; therefore, having established you in my own heart-lotus, I shall offer libations. Having thus requested permission and entered the form of the Fire through the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*), one should [offer] into his heart-lotus: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dharma. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Jñāna. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vairāgya. (6) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aiśvarya. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Padma. Having thus worshipped the seat, [one worships] upon it: Oṃ heṃ, salutation to the seat of Tatpuruṣa-Śiva. The meditation:
[One should visualize] a man resembling gold, wearing yellow garments and a sacred thread.
Holding a citron and a rosary, and likewise adorned with a moon upon his crest—
one should worship the Nara-mantra in the eastern Veda-triangular sacrificial pit.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the form of Tatpuruṣa-Śiva*. (3) *Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa-Śiva*. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), (4) having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), and having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, flowers, garlands, and so forth, one should worship with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra. (5) One should display the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*). To the north of Tatpuruṣa: *Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the seat of the tongue of the weapon (*astrajihvāsana*)*.
The visualization (*dhyāna*): (6) four-faced, four-armed, fanged, and of tawny luster.

Facing Śiva, one should worship the Astra [deity] in the eastern *kuṇḍa*, and the Puruṣa [deity] to the north, [visualizing him] as endowed with the spear, the shield, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.

Having thus meditated: "Oṃ haḥ, obeisance to the form of Astra-Śiva; Oṃ (2) haḥ, obeisance to the form of Astra-Śiva," and having performed the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), one should offer incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra, one should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra-mudrā*). Then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth—

For the purpose of satiating the mantra, having offered one hundred oblations each with the two mantras of Tatpuruṣa and Astra, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer four hundred oblations each with the same two mantras as before for the sake of averting ill omens related to the location, the time, and the fuel-wood, and for the purpose of attaining auspiciousness; then, having offered the full oblation, one offers one hundred oblations each as a constituent part of the ritual of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*); and finally, having offered the full oblation, [one recites]: *oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣaśivāya svāhā*.

*Oṃ haḥ astraśivāya svāhā*—with this single oblation, perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Having performed the kindling (*dīpana*) with three oblations using *oṃ hūṃ heṃ hūṃ tatpuruṣāya huṃ phaṭ*, and having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), [one offers] *oṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having offered one hundred oblations each with *palāśa* wood fuel using the two aforementioned mantras as before, and likewise with sacrificial substances such as barley and so forth in the same number—or according to one's capacity—one offers: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*.

Oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā | Having thus offered four oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the materials, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the Guru first offers the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), gives water for rinsing the mouth, betel, and so forth, and having reported the recitation (*japa*), he pays homage. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the eastern fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).

(i.41b *dakṣiṇakuṇḍavidhiḥ*) Now, the procedure for the southern fire-pit (*dakṣiṇakuṇḍa*) is described: the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having sat facing north on the southern side of the pit for the purpose of lying down in the form of a eunuch and drawing the bow, perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the four paths. Then the Guru, having taken the fire from the principal pit into a shallow dish (*śarāva*) on its southern side and having cast it into the southern pit, the officiating priests kindle the fire.

For the purpose of protecting the fire, having spread darbha grass blades with their tips pointing toward the northeast on the eastern girdle and so forth, using [mantras] ending in *astra*, and having likewise placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them: In the east: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. In the west: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*. In the north: *oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus for the *jyā* [sticks]. On the sacrificial seats, starting from the east and ending with the north: *indrāya namaḥ*; *agnaye namaḥ*.

Salutation to Yama; salutation to Nairṛta; salutation to Varuṇa; salutation to Vāyu; salutation to Kubera; salutation to Īśāna; (3) salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya*, and having requested [the deities] for the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), the spoon (*sruva*), and the clarified butter (*ājya*).
And having meditated upon the fire in this manner—as possessing three eyes and the weapons of Śiva as its jewel-like arms—one should recite:
"O Fire, you are the lordly splendor, since you are the supreme purifier. (5)
Therefore, having established [thee] within the lotus of my heart, I satisfy thee.

Having thus informed [the deity] (I.42b), [the practitioner], having caused the fire-form to enter the central channel, [worships] in its heart-lotus: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairājñā(ya) namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped the seat, [he worships] above that: *oṃ hāṃ aghoraśivāya namaḥ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
"The supreme [deity] has three eyes, is endowed with a moon upon his crown, and is adorned with earrings. (4)
With a tawny beard and hair, fanged and with a distorted face.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with snakes and scorpions,
he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, a skull-cup, a shield, and a noose.
In the four left hands and the four right hands,
[he holds] a trident, an axe, a sword, and a staff that crushes enemies.
Thus, Aghora shines like a fresh cloud, granting all desires;
a wise person should worship Aghora in the southern bow-shaped sacrificial pit.

Having meditated thus: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one whose form is Aghora; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aghora-Śiva*. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), and having adorned [the deity] with water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance (*gandha*), unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), garlands of flowers (*puṣpadāma*), and so forth; and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should display the trident mudrā (*triśūlamudrā*). Then, having offered incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), and the like, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire.

Having offered one hundred oblations with its root mantra for the purpose of satisfying the mantra, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of special satisfaction, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations each with the root mantra for the sake of pacifying ill omens regarding the attainment of place (*deśāpādana*) and time (*kālāpādana*), and for the attainment of auspicious omens, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra as an ancillary part of the rite of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*), and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*—the satisfaction is performed with: *oṃ huṃ aghoraśivāya svāhā*. Thus is the satisfaction.

Oṃ hūṃ huṃ hūṃ (3) aghoraśivāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā. With these three oblations, one should perform the kindling (*dīpana*). Then, having offered a hundred oblations with *audumbara* wood using the mantra "oṃ huṃ aghoraśivāya svāhā," and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer oblations of mung beans and other sacrificial materials as before, either according to the prescribed number or according to one's capacity. [Then recite: "oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā; oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā; oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā."

"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati! Having thus offered four oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the ritual substances, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having offered the *caru* preceded by the Guru, and having given water for rinsing the mouth, betel, and so forth; and having performed the recitation (*japa*), the offering, and the prostration—thus concludes the procedure for the worship of the southern sacrificial pit (*dakṣiṇakuṇḍa*).

Now, the procedure for the northern pit (*uttarakuṇḍa*) is described: the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), seated facing east on the western side of the lotus-shaped pit which has a female form, perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the four paths (as stated in i.44b). Then, the Guru, having taken the fire from the central pit using a shallow dish (*śarāva*) from its northern side and having cast it into the northern pit, the officiating priests kindle the fire.

For the purpose of protecting the fire, having spread darbha grass with their tips pointing northeast upon the eastern girdles using the Astra-mantra, and having likewise arranged the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them; [one should worship] on the enclosing sticks—on the east: *Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; on the west: *Viṣṇave namaḥ*; on the south: *Oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the north: *Oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. (Having thus worshipped), [one worships] on the sacrificial seats from the east to the northeast: *Oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nairṛta. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. (I.45a) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna. To the south of that: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā. To the north of Nairṛta: (2) homage to Viṣṇu. Thus [performing] the *jya* [offering]. Having offered the *arghya*, and having requested the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

In the principal *kuṇḍa*, having placed the well-prepared clarified butter (*ājya*)—which has undergone the consecration (*saṃskāra*)—into a shallow dish (*śarāva-pātra*) by means of the teacher’s hand, and taking it up, he should hold it over the navel of the *kuṇḍa*. Having placed two *darbha* blades with their tips joined and a knot in the middle, measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length, into the midst of the ghee while reciting the *praṇava*; having consecrated it with the *Vāmadeva* mantra, protected it, and veiled it; and having rendered it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), he should worship it.
Then, having meditated upon the Fire in this manner: "He possesses a body of jewels, three eyes, and arms endowed with the weapons of Śiva" (I.45b). Thus one should meditate on the Fire.

"O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, for you are the supreme purifier; therefore, having established [the deity] within the lotus of your heart, I offer libations. (2) Having thus requested permission from Agni and entered through the central channel (*nāḍī*) into the middle of his form, one worships the seat in his heart-lotus with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dharma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jñāna. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vairājya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Padma. (4) Having thus worshipped the seat, one worships upon it: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāmadeva."
Dhyāna—The left [hand] is red, with a very bright luster, adorned with a garland, garments, and a sacred thread;
it has a prominent nose and a reddish uṣṇīṣa, and holds a sword and a shield. (5)

In the northern lotus-pool, one should worship Vāmadeva. Having meditated thus: (6) *oṃ hīṃ vāmadevaśivamūrtaye namaḥ* | *oṃ hīṃ vāmadevaśivāya namaḥ* | having offered the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the water-offering (*arghya*); having adorned him with perfumes, garlands of flowers, and so forth; having worshipped him with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra; one should display the *makara-mudrā*. Then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and the like, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire.
