Having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of satiating the mantras, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of special satiation, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations each with the root mantra for the sake of pacifying ill omens arising from place or time, and for the attainment of auspicious omens, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra as a constituent part of the ritual of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*), and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*—the satiation is performed with a single oblation: *Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevaśivāya svāhā*.

Oṃ hūṃ hīṃ hūṃ vāmadevāya huṃ phaṭ. With these three oblations, one should perform the kindling (*dīpana*). Then, with the mantra "Oṃ hīṃ vāmadevaguhyāya svāhā," one should offer a hundred oblations of *vaṭa* wood. Having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer chickpeas and other sacrificial materials (*homadravya*) as before, either in the prescribed number or according to one's capacity. [Then offer: Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā; Oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā; Oṃ hāṃ sūrpāya svāhā; Oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā.

Thus, having offered the four *vyāhṛti* oblations at the end of the materials, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having offered the *caru* preceded by the Guru, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*), betel, and so forth, having performed the recitation (*japa*), having presented the offering (*nivedya*), and having prostrated—thus ends the procedure for the northern sacrificial pit (*uttarakuṇḍavidhi*).

(i.47a *paścimakuṇḍavidhi*) Now the procedure for the western fire-pit (*paścimakuṇḍavidhi*) is described: The officiant (*ṛtvij*), seated facing east on the western side of the circular pit which has the form of a woman, performs the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the four paths. The Guru, having taken the fire from the western side of the principal pit in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), places it into the western pit. The officiant kindles the fire and, for the protection of the fire, spreads darbha grass with their tips pointing northeast upon the eastern girdle (*mekhalā*) using the *astra-mantra*.

Having established the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) in their respective places: on the enclosing sticks—on the east, *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; on the west, *viṣṇave namaḥ*; on the south, *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the north, *oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus for the enclosing sticks. On the grass seats—from the east to the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ nairṛte namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. (2) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped them and offered the *arghya* water, (3) having requested the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should take the clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been consecrated by the Guru in the primary sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), place it in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), and, taking it with the Guru’s hand, (4) place it at the navel of the pit.

Having placed a *prādeśamātra* [measure] made of two tips of *darbha* grass with two *kuśa* blades tied by a central knot into the midst of the clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*, having consecrated it with the *sadyojāta* mantra, protected it, and veiled it; having rendered it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) with the *dhenumudrā* using that same mantra, and having worshipped it—having thus meditated upon the fire as the Jewel-Body (*ratnatanu*), endowed with arms bearing the weapons of Śiva such as the trident and the axe—one should say:
"O Fire, you are the splendor of Īśvara, for you are the supreme purifier. (I.48a)
"Therefore, having firmly established [thee] within the lotus of my heart, I shall offer libations.

Having thus requested this command from Agni, one enters his form through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) and, in his heart-lotus, worships the seat with: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Upon that, one worships: *oṃ hāṃ sadyojātaśivāsanāya namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Abundantly adorned with white garlands, sandalwood paste, and ornaments, wearing a white turban and white garments, gentle,
endowed with a crescent moon upon his crown, having the form of a youth, and possessing three eyes— Sadyojāta, who has one white face and hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (5)

In the western circular pit, [one worships] Sadyojāta... (i.48b). Now, the procedure for the southeastern pit is described: the officiant, seated facing north on the southern side of the womb-pit (*yonikuṇḍa*) which has the form of a woman, performs the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the four paths. Having taken the fire from the southern side of the principal pit into a shallow dish (*śarāva*), and having placed it into the southeastern pit, the officiant kindles the fire.

For the purpose of protecting the fire, having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the northeast upon the eastern and other girdles (*mekhalā*) using the *astra-mantra*, and having likewise placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them: [one should worship] on the enclosing sticks—on the east: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; on the west: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; on the south: *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the north: *oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus for the enclosing sticks. On the sacrificial seats—from the east to the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Agni. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nairṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu. Thus [one performs] the *jya* [offering]. Having offered the *arghya*, and having requested [the protection of] Agni for the sake of guarding [the ritual site], one performs the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

Having taken the clarified butter (*ājya*)—which has undergone the ritual purification (*saṃskāra*) performed by the Guru—in the *pradhānakuṇḍa* from a shallow dish (*śarāva*) using the Guru’s hand, and holding it over the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should place two blades of *darbha* grass, each a span (*prādeśa*) long, with their tips joined and tied together at the middle with a knot, into the midst of the ghee while reciting the *praṇava*. Having consecrated it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, protected it, and veiled it, one should transform it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenumudrā* while reciting that same mantra.
Then, having worshipped it and meditated upon the fire as being red in color, three-eyed, and endowed with arms bearing the weapons of Śiva—one should proceed.
O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor, for you are the supreme purifier;
therefore, having established you within the lotus of my heart, I offer libations to you.

Having thus requested permission from the Fire-god, one enters the central channel (*madhyanāḍī*) and, within his heart-lotus, worships the seat with: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Then, upon that, [one worships] with: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayaśivāsanāya namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*):
the heart is like the moon and is enveloped in white cloth.
Seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of matted hair marked by a crescent moon,
three-eyed, four-armed, and adorned with all ornaments;
facing Śiva, he holds a spear, a trident, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.

One should worship the Heart-mantra in the *yonikuṇḍa* in the southeast. Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, the embodiment of the Heart; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva of the Heart," one should offer the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), as well as water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. One should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*). Having offered incense, lamps, food offerings, and so on, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire. Then, for the purpose of satiating the mantra, one should perform a hundred oblations using its root-mantra.

Having offered the *pūrṇā* oblation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the sake of special satisfaction. Having offered the *pūrṇā*, one should offer a hundred oblations each with the root mantra for the purpose of averting ill omens arising from the place or the time, and for securing auspicious omens. Having offered the *pūrṇā*, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra as an ancillary part of the ritual of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*). Having offered the *pūrṇā*: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart"—with this, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed. With three oblations using "Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ hūṃ, hūṃ phaṭ, svāhā to the heart," one should perform the kindling (*dīpana*).

(5) Then, having offered one hundred oblations with *śamī* fuel sticks while reciting the mantra *oṃ hṛdayāya svāhā*, and having offered oblation substances such as sesame seeds (*tila*) and others in the same number as before—or according to one's capacity—reciting: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā* (i.51a), he should offer four oblations of the *vyāhṛti*s at the conclusion of the substances, and then present the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). The Guru, having first offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), given water for rinsing the mouth, betel, and so forth, performed the recitation (*japa*), presented the offering (*naivedya*), and paid obeisance; thus ends the ritual procedure for the worship and oblation in the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*).

(i.51b The Procedure for the Nairṛta Pit) Now, the procedure for the Nairṛta pit is described: the presiding priest (mūrtipa), seated facing east on the western side of the triangular pit which has the form of a woman, performs the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the pit, beginning with its inspection and ending with the laying of the crossroads. Then the Guru, having taken fire from the southwest quarter of the principal pit into a shallow bowl (śarāva), places it into the Nairṛta pit. The presiding priest then kindles the fire.

For the protection of the fire, having strewn *darbha* grass with its tips pointing toward the northeast upon the eastern girdles (*mekhalā*) using the *astra-mantra*, and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them, one should offer oblations (*jyā*) to the enclosing sticks as follows: in the east—*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; in the west—*oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; in the south—*oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; in the north—*oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Then, on the sacrificial seats from the east to the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Nairṛta. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Īśāna. To the south: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā. Between Nairṛta and the north: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya* water, and having requested [them] for the protection of the fire, one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and spoon (*sruva*).

In the primary sacrificial pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*), having performed the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*) by the Guru, and having taken the clarified butter from the vessel (*śarāva-pātra*) with his own hand, he places it in the center of the pit. Having placed two *kuśa* blades—one a span (*prādeśa*) long with two tips, and another with a knot in the middle—into the midst of the ghee while reciting the *praṇava*, he consecrates it with the *śikhā-mantra*. Having protected it and veiled it, he renders it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) with the *dhenu-mudrā* using that same mantra. Having worshipped it, he meditates upon the fire as follows:
"And He [the Fire] possesses a body of jewels, three eyes, and arms endowed with the weapons of Śiva. Thus he meditates on the fire.
O Agni, you are the sovereign splendor and the supreme purifier;
therefore, having established you within the lotus of my heart, I offer you satisfaction.

Having thus requested permission from the Fire-form (*agnivigraha*), one enters his heart-lotus through the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). There, one worships the seat with: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairājyāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Upon that [seat], one worships: *oṃ hūṃ śikhāśivāsanāya namaḥ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[One visualizes] the crest (*śikhā*) resembling vermilion (*sindūra*), encircled by red garments.
Seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of matted hair adorned with the crescent moon,
three-eyed, four-armed, and decorated with all ornaments;
facing Śiva, he holds a spear, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
"In a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the southwest, one should worship the mantras of the *śikhā* [crown].

Having thus meditated: "Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva as the *śikhā*; Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Śiva as the *śikhā*. Having thus performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and confinement (*sannirodhana*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*), and having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken grains, garlands of flowers, and so forth, and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers using that mantra, and having displayed the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*), then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so on, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire.

Having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of satisfying the mantras, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of special satisfaction, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations each with the root mantra for the sake of pacifying ill omens occurring at the time of entering the site or entering the dwelling, and for the sake of securing auspicious omens, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra as a subsidiary part of the ritual of sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*), and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*—one performs the satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*) with: *oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai svāhā*.

One should perform the kindling with three oblations using the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ huṃ hūṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having offered one hundred oblations of *khadira* wood with the mantra *oṃ huṃ śikhāya svāhā*, and having offered oblation materials such as black gram (*māṣa*) and so forth, either in the aforementioned number or according to one's capacity, as before; and then, having offered the four *vyāhṛti* oblations: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā*.

Having offered the *caru* oblation preceded by the Guru, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*), betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), and so forth, and having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the offering (*nivedya*),
[one proceeds with] the ritual for the wind-pit (*vāyukuṇḍavidhi*).

Now, the procedure for the wind-pit (*vāyukuṇḍa*) is described: the presiding priest (*mūrtipa*), assuming the form of a man, sits facing east on the western side of the white hexagonal pit. Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with the inspection of the pit and ending with the fourfold path, the Guru takes the fire from the wind-quarter in the primary pit using a shallow dish (*śarāva*). Having placed it in the wind-pit, the presiding priest kindles the fire. For the protection of the fire, he spreads *darbha* grass with their tips pointing northeast upon the eastern girdle (*mekhalā*) using the *astra-mantra*.

Having likewise placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the seats (*viṣṭara*) among them, one should worship as follows: on the enclosing sticks—on the east, *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; on the west, *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; on the south, *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya namaḥ*; on the north, *oṃ hāṃ īśvarāya namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] on the seats from the east to the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ nairṛte namaḥ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Thus [perform] the *jya* [offering]. Having offered the *arghya*, having requested the protection of the fire, and having performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should take the clarified butter (*ājya*)—which has been consecrated by the Guru—in a shallow dish (*śarāva*) from the hand of the Guru and place it at the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

(4) Having placed two *kuśa* blades—one at each end and one in the middle tied with a knot—measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length, into the midst of the clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava* (Oṃ); having consecrated them with the *kavaca* mantra; having protected and concealed them; having rendered them nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the *dhenumudrā* with that same mantra; and having worshipped them;
(5–6) having thus meditated upon the fire as being endowed with arms holding the *ratnatatra*, the three eyes, and the weapons of Śiva;
[one should say: "O Fire, you are the purifying splendor of Īśvara for me who am striving."

"Therefore, having established [the deity] within the lotus of your heart, I shall offer libations. Having thus requested this command, one enters the form of Agni through the central channel (*madhya-nāḍī*). Within his heart-lotus, one worships the seat as follows: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vairājñāya (vairāgyāya) namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ*. Then, upon that, one worships: *oṃ hauṃ kavaca-śivāsanāya namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Wearing armor with the luster of a bumblebee and draped in divine garments, he is seated upon a lotus, bearing a crown of matted hair marked by the crescent moon;
he has three eyes, four arms, and is adorned with all ornaments. (4)

Facing Śiva, [the wise one] should worship the Armour (Kavaca), which is endowed with the spear, the trident, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, in the north-western corner of the hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). (5)

Having meditated thus: *oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor (*kavaca*) of the Śiva-form; oṃ haiṃ (6) oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the armor-Śiva*. Having thus performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering (*arghya*); having adorned [the deity] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), garlands of flowers, and so forth; and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) using that mantra, one should display the gesture of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*). Then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so on, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire.

Having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of satisfying the mantras, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of special satisfaction, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations each with the root mantra for the sake of attaining the pacification of unfavorable signs and the attainment of favorable signs regarding the location and the time, and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*; having offered one hundred oblations with the root mantra as an ancillary part of the sprinkling rite (*prokṣaṇa*), and having given the *pūrṇāhuti*—[one performs] the satisfaction [with the mantra]: *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya svāhā*.

One should perform the kindling (*dīpana*) with three oblations using the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ haiṃ hūṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ*. [The wood for the fuel is] from the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees. Then, having offered one hundred oblations of *aśvattha* fuel sticks with the mantra *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya svāhā*, and having offered one hundred oblations—or as many as possible according to one's capacity—of sacrificial materials such as *kuluttha* beans and so forth, as before, [one offers]: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā*.

"Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Prajāpati. Having offered these four oblations, having offered the *caru* to the lineage of gurus, having given water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), betel, and so forth, and having performed the recitation (*japa*), the offering (*nivedya*), and the prostration—the ritual procedure for the worship and fire-offering (*havana*) in the Vāyu-pit is completed. Regarding the wood for the sacrificial pits: *Aśvattha*, *Udumbara*, *Plakṣa*, and *Vaṭa* are for the directions starting from the east; *Śamī*, *Khadira*, *Māyūra*, and *Plakṣa* are for the corners starting from the southeast. However, for the principal pit, *Pālāśa* wood should be used, and that is approved everywhere. (Kāmika Tantra, Chapter on the Installation of the Śiva-liṅga, verse 56b).
The eight forms— earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind, the moon, and space— should be installed.
The fierce Rudra is the obstructer within the sphere of Nirukti;
Mahādeva, the Lord of Existence, and Bhīma—these are the eight guardians of the Mūrtis.
Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, Balotkaṭā,
Dhātrī, and Vihruti are proclaimed as the attendants of the Goddess who guard her forms.
The Guru should offer oblations with the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
likewise, for the limbs [of the mantra], it should be one-tenth of the root, or equal to it, or half of that.
The oblation for the deities of the forms (mūrtipāhuti) is prescribed with the Brahma-mantras in the eight directions;
in the northeast and the four directions starting from the east, the Brahma-mantras are the heart and the others.

In the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛti, and Vāyu, respectively, one should satisfy the mantras at the conclusion of the *pūrṇāhuti* offerings; or, if Īśāna is the principal deity, [one satisfies] the Eye and the Weapon mantras in the central *kuṇḍa*. Then, [one offers] jars filled with pure water.
One should fashion [them] obtained from a hundred weapons, consecrated by the completion of the mantra-ritual.
The peaceful water-pot (*śāntikumbha*) is the cause for the presence of the *Sruvāriśānti*;
it belongs to the preceptor (*ācārya*), who performs more recitations (*japa*) with the root mantra and the *Aṇusaṃhitā* mantras.
The Guru should perform the worship of Śiva along with His limbs (aṅgas) in the principal sacrificial pit (pradhānakuṇḍa).
The wise one [should recite] the three mantras: Īśāna, Netra, and Śiras.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the Īśāna-pit (northeast pit), the wise one should worship Puruṣa in the eastern pit and Astra in its left [corner], in their respective places. (4)
One should worship the Heart-mantra in the southeast fire-pit, Aghora in the south, the Śikhā-mantra in the southwest, and Sadyojāta in the west. (5)
One should worship the Kavaca mantra in the Vāyu-kunda and the Vāmadeva mantra in the northern [kunda].
One should honor the officiating priests and offer mantras, incense, lamps, and other such items.

(i.57b *navakuṇḍavidhi*) Having gone near the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), the image-protectors (*mūrtipāḥ*), by the command of the Guru, shall each approach their own pit and perform the consecration of the pit (*kuṇḍasaṃskṛti*). The Guru, as previously described, having completed the ritual of the pit’s consecration ending with the naming of the fire, shall divide the fire into nine parts—or five—and cast them into the respective pits according to their directions. Then, having divided the fire for the sake of the sacrificial pap (*caru*), he shall lift it up, preserve a portion for the hearth (*culī*), and kindle the middle portion.

Having performed the *idhmahoma* and worshipped the Blessed One in the center of the fire, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the mantra. The image-guardians (*mūrtipās*) should also worship in the fire for the protection of their respective mantras; having performed the mantra-libation and offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should then offer one hundred oblations for each with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) for the purpose of pacifying unfavorable signs related to place, time, and circumstance, and for securing auspicious signs. Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) as before, one should present it as an offering.
Having consecrated the *śāntikumbha* jars with the Astra-mantra by reciting it one hundred times and having performed the *saṃpāta* oblation, they should proceed to the bathing pavilion.
Meditation on the Lord of the Form (*mūrtyadhipati*):
[He is] golden-colored, with a most beautiful face, holding a deer, an axe, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands.
I meditate upon Śiva, whose deity is Śarva, the lord of the earth and the forms, situated in the eastern direction. 1.

I meditate upon the Lord of the form of Fire, the master of the self and the lord of the quarters, who stands in the south-eastern direction; he holds a deer, a chisel, and the gestures of boon and fearlessness in his hands, possesses the color of fire, and has an exceedingly beautiful face. 2.

I meditate upon Śiva, who stands to the right, blue in color with an exceedingly beautiful face, holding a deer, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness in his hands; he is the fierce deity, the presiding lord of the form of the sacrificer. 3.

I meditate upon Śiva, who stands in the southwest, holding a deer, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness in his hands; he is the color of a bumblebee, possesses an exceedingly beautiful face, and has the Sun, the Moon, and Rudra as his presiding deities. 4.

I bring before you Śiva, who stands in the western quarter, holding a deer, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands; he is moon-colored, possesses an exceedingly beautiful face, and is the leader of the water-forms of the world and the gods. ||5||

I meditate upon the Lord whose deity is Īśa, the master of the form of Vāyu, who stands in the direction of Śiva and Vāyu, holding a deer, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness in his hands, clad in white armor, and possessing an exceedingly beautiful face. (6)

I meditate upon Śiva, who stands in the northern direction, red in color with an exceedingly beautiful face, holding a deer, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands, and whose leader is Mahādeva bearing the moon on his crest. 7.

I meditate upon the deity Śiva, who stands in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), white in color with an exceedingly beautiful face, holding in his hands the deer, the axe, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; he resembles the form of the sky. (i.58b) The weapon-mantra of Śiva: Oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.

The Aghorāstra mantra: *oṃ sphura sphura prasphura prasphura ghora ghoratanu rūpa tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa | kaha kaha — vama vama — bandhaya bandhaya — ghātaya ghātaya — oṃ huṃ aghorāstrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Pāśupatāstra mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ baṃ śuṃ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

The *Pratyaṅgirā* Weapon-mantra: *Oṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ rudrāsthiśriṅkhale huṃ sarvato bhadre kuṭirudrivacana-vidāri rakṣa rakṣa māṃ pratyaṅgire | dhāma dhāma jyoti jyoti suve suvaḥ bhuve bhuvaḥ pāhyamṛto'haṃ satyahantribhidan pādo juṣā lakṣmi namo vaḥ kirikeyaṃ karoti tamo vāñcha viśaja mahādeva suvrato namaḥ svāhā |* The *Mṛtyuñjaya* Weapon-mantra: *Oṃ juṃ saḥ mṛtyuñjayāstrāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā |*
The Kṣurikā weapon mantra: *oṃ kṣuṃ kṣurikā-āyudhāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Śivasāvitrī: *oṃ vyoma-vyomāya vidmahe sūkṣma-sūkṣmāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt svāhā*.
The Śivagāyatrī: *oṃ tanmaheśāya vidmahe vāgviśuddhāya dhīmahi tannaḥ śivaḥ pracodayāt svāhā*.

Having offered one hundred oblations into the principal fire-pit with the root mantra and having presented the full-offering (*pūrṇāhuti*), they should offer [oblations] into the four pits starting from the east with the [mantras of] Śarva and the others, into those starting from the southeast with Tatpuruṣa and the others, and into the principal pit with Hṛdaya and the others. They should also offer the Eye of Īśāna; one should perform the homa with the remaining materials.
One should offer the Aśvattha tree and wheat into the eastern pit.
One should offer fuel-sticks and mustard seeds with the *hṛdaya* mantra into the fire-pit in the southeast;
likewise, one should offer sesame and *audumbara* wood with the *aghora* mantra into the southern pit.
With the *śikhā* mantra, one should offer *khādira* and *pāṭalī* materials into the southwestern pit.
In the west, one should offer *plakṣa* and *mudga* with the Sadyojāta mantra;
in the northwest, one should offer *balva* and *caṇaka* with the Kavaca mantra;
and in the north, one should offer *āḍhaka* and *vaṭa* with the Vāmadeva mantra.
In the northeast, one should offer arka and māṣa with the Śira-mantra;
in the principal fire-pit, one should offer clarified butter with the Mūla-mantra one hundred times.

One should offer parched grain with the *puruṣa* mantra, *prayaṅgu* with the root mantra, sesame with the *vāma* mantra, and white mustard seeds with the *pāśupata* mantra, using the *śiras* mantra [for each]. (3)

One should offer black gram with the *hṛdaya* mantra, green gram with the *mūla* mantra, peas and horse-gram with the *netra* mantra, barley with the *īśāna* mantra, and rice with the *śāliśira* mantra.

With the root-mantra, one should offer wild rice (*nīvāra*), cultivated rice (*vrīhi*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *hyāmaka*, *āraḍhaka*, *niṣpāvaka*, *veṇka*, wheat (*godhūma*), curd, musk (*kastūrī*), sandalwood (*candana*), camphor (*karpūra*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), black aloe (*kṛṣṇagandha*), yellow pigment (*gorocana*), the two types of musk (*mṛgamada*), snow-water (*himatoya*), *śrīvera*, guggulu resin, and so forth; with the root-mantra, sugar-cane pieces, their own tubers and so forth, plantain fruits and so forth, mango fruits, jackfruit, jaggery, and so forth—with the *aghora* mantra; and betel-leaf with the root-mantra—or one should offer each of these oblation substances individually one hundred times, or half that amount.

Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations at the conclusion of each respective substance, the Guru then offers clarified butter (*ājya*) one thousand, five hundred, or one hundred times with the root mantra.
(3) (The procedure for the eightfold binding:
Having smeared with cow dung, he prepares a square area before the deity.
One should sprinkle both the mortar and the pestle with pure water.
Having worshipped the sixfold Āsana, one should place them upon it;
the mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the pestle has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
Having adorned the mortar and pestle with garments and *darbha* grass, there should be plantain, powdered conch-shell, lac, and likewise *guggulu*;
sugar mixed with honey, cotton, and sesame oil as well. (6)
One should cause these to be made in equal proportions for the eightfold binding.
Mahimā, butter, as well as powdered guggulu, combined with cotton and lac, one should cause to be made into a fivefold binding. (I.60b)
Powder combined with guggulu and mixed with fresh butter—this should be meditated upon as the "threefold bond" (*tribandhana*); indeed, the bond is both matured and un-matured.
Having gathered [the ingredients] together with the practitioner and the master according to the sequence of binding—
one part of the powder and one part of guggulu—
these should be mixed with fresh butter for immediate crushing and binding.
Plantain, fresh butter, and cotton—each measuring one foot; likewise, bdellium and molasses, each measuring one mātra and being sweet and pure.
Two types of lac combined with three kinds of stone powder—this is declared to be the "eightfold binding" (*aṣṭabandhana*); one should apply it according to the oral instructions.
Cotton, sesame seeds, buffalo ghee, and sugar are [substitutes] for lac;
resin and bitumen are [substitutes] for guggulu and for the mineral dyes.
The eightfold binding of the linga and the pedestal within the cavity is common [to all].
Having performed the rites of the eightfold binding, one should then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Having offered incense, lamps, and the fivefold food offering (*pañcanivedya*) according to the sequence of the honors (*upacāra*), one should then go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having performed the oblation (*homa*) with the *vyāhṛtis* as an auxiliary to the eight-fold binding rite (*aṣṭabandhakarma*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra, together with the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the southern side of the consecration altar (*pratiṣṭhāvedikā*), one should place upon it the peace-vessel (*śāntikumbha*)—a jar equal in number to the officiating preceptors (*ācārya*), equipped with thread and cloth, provided with a lid, containing gold and gems, and furnished with a ritual grass-bundle (*kūrca*).

Having invoked Śiva into the form of the seat upon that [altar], and having worshipped him with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, one should consecrate [the materials] a hundred times with the Astra-mantra. Having offered incense and lamps, one should then offer the special substances for the fire-sacrifice (*homa*). One should offer *aśvattha* wood, wheat, and *puruṣa* (human hair) into the eastern pit; at the conclusion of the substances, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, the guardians of the forms—whether eight or four—should likewise offer into their respective pits and present the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Having worshipped the peace-pitchers (*śāntikalaśa*) and others in the directions starting from the east—in the southeast, northeast, and northwest—one should complete the rite.

In the center—at the region of the navel—one should offer salutation with "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kriyāśakti. Then, in their respective places, having worshipped Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others (three), one should worship their own individual forms and the form of the seat with the root mantra, in the sequence starting from the east, by means of invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), confinement (*sannirodhana*), binding of the directions (*dikbandhana*), veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and so forth.

Afterwards, having worshipped with *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai namaḥ* (5), and having offered three oblations with *oṃ hlāṃ nivṛttikalāyai svāhā*, one should then offer: *oṃ hāṃ pṛthivī-tattvāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ pṛthivī-tattvādhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ* (6); and afterwards, *oṃ hāṃ ātma-tattvāya svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ ātma-tattvādhipataye brahmaṇe svāhā*. (i.62a) Having thus given these three oblations, [one offers]: *āṃ hīṃ vidyā-tattvāya namaḥ*.

Having offered three oblations with the mantras: *oṃ hīṃ vidyātatvādhipataye viṣṇave svāhā*, *oṃ hūṃ śivatatvāya svāhā*, and *oṃ hūṃ śivatatvādhipataye rudrāya svāhā*, one should—by means of the yoga of unification through the flower-vase and hook mudrās—join the deity residing in the image, the fire, the heart, the center of the altar, and the water-pot with the Śiva residing in the fire. Then, the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipas*) likewise perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).

Then, in the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) of the east, south, north, and west, one should offer oblations one hundred times each with the root mantras of the Śivāstra, Aghorāstra, Pāśupatāstra, and Mūla-mantra; and in the fire-pits of the southeast and so forth, one should offer oblations one hundred times each with the Aghorāstra, Sāvitrī-gāyatrī, and Pratyaṅgirā-āstra mantras.
[The meditation on the Earth-form (Kṣmāmūrti):
eight-armed, four-faced, wearing yellow garments...
He is seated upon a tortoise, possesses a gentle form, is fragrant, and is surrounded by water.
One should worship the Earth-form (Kṣmāmūrti) of the God [in the east]... (2) The meditation on the Fire-form (Vahnimūrti):
mounted upon a ram, red in color, and equipped with a spear and a lance.
In the southeast, he is adorned with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and has the form of fire.
(3) In the south, he has the form of the sacrificer; he is one-faced and three-eyed, holding a deer, an axe, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
With his limbs smeared with fresh butter, the sacrificer possesses a beautiful form;
he is the embodiment of the Sun, mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, wearing armor and red earrings.
One should visualize the form of Arka wearing a crown and holding a lotus in his hand.
(5) The form of Jala is four-armed, white in color, and adorned with all ornaments.
In the west is the one in the form of water, situated in a crocodile, holding a noose in his hand.
[Then] the one in the form of wind, four-armed, four-faced, smoke-colored, and of great strength.
One should meditate upon the form of Vāyu, joined with a fluttering banner;
[and] the form of Indu, resembling pure crystal, with two lotuses in his two hands. (6) (2)
One should visualize him with one face, residing in a celestial chariot, having the form of the moon.
[Verse 7] One should also visualize the form of space as four-armed and four-faced, holding a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and a trident (*triśūla*).
One should always remember him as having the form of space, holding a conch shell and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hands. 8.
(i.63b) The fire-differentiation meditation consists of the meditation on the child-fire,
which has two faces, one heart, four ears, and two nostrils.
He has four horns, is mounted upon a bull, and possesses a radiance equal to the rising sun.

In his right side [hands] are a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a spoon (*sruva*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), and a spear (*śakti*); in his left side [hands] are a lance (*tomara*), a fan (*vyajana*), and a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛtapātra*).
One should meditate on the form of the fire of childhood in this way, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
(3) [Next,] one should meditate on the fire of youth as having three eyes, five faces, red limbs, and ten hands.

In the right [hands], he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a vajra; in the left [hands], he holds a chisel, a noose, a lotus, a wheel, and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). (4–2)
Vṛddhāgni has four arms and three eyes, one face, and wears matted hair;
he holds a trident and an axe, and is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
One should meditate upon the white lotus and the aged Agni mounted upon a bull.
(6) The Gārhapatya fire has red limbs and wears red garments, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

One should meditate upon Gārhapatya, who bestows the accomplishment of all aims: he holds a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle with his raised right hand, is adorned with ornaments of pearls, possesses seven tongues of flame, has one face, wears matted hair, and is mounted upon a horse. 4.
The Āhavanīya fire has one face and three eyes; it possesses three girdles and three feet.
In its right hands, it holds a rosary, a trident, and a *sruva* ladle. (3)
In his left hands he holds a hook, a hand-drum, and a sacrificial ladle;
he is red in color, seated comfortably, and draped in yellow garments.
One should meditate upon the Āhavanīya fire for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
The Dakṣiṇāgni fire has two faces, the luster of gold, three feet, and seven hands;
it possesses four tongues, beginning with Hiraṇyā, in its right face. (5)

The three tongues, Suprabhā and the others, are situated in the left face. He holds a spear (*śakti*) and a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) in his right hands, and a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛtapātra*) in his left.
He carries a javelin (*tomara*) and an axe (*paraśu*) in his [other] left hands, and is mounted upon a goat (*aja*) as his vehicle.
Meditating upon the Dakṣiṇāgni as the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and purposes—
[he is] the solitary Fire,
with two eyes and two arms, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Equipped with pure garments, he was adorned with white and red [attire].
Having meditated upon [the deity] as being endowed with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, and consisting solely of fire— which grants the accomplishment of all desires and aims— (7).

The common fire-god has two faces; he holds a Veda, a horn, the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), and a spoon (*sruva*) in his right and left hands, and carries the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and a shield (*kheṭa*) in his upper right and left hands.

One should meditate upon the nature of the universal fire (*sāmānyāgni*), which bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (8) Regarding the system of five sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*): one should perform the *homa* starting from the east—[offering] to Tatpuruṣa with the Heart-mantra in the east; to Aghora with the Head-mantra in the south; to Vāmadeva with the Crest-mantra in the north; and to Sadyojāta with the Armor-mantra in the west. In the northeast, one should perform the *homa* for the principal pit (*pradhānakuṇḍa*) to Īśāna with the Eye-mantra and the Weapon-mantra (*astra*). For the [four] directions starting from the east, one should offer oblations with wood from the *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees. For the directions starting from the east, one should perform the *homa* with *śamī*, *khadira*, *silkā*, and *arka* wood. One should perform the *homa* in the principal pit using *pālāśa* wood.

Having offered a thousand oblations with the root mantra, along with five hundred, one hundred, and the Brahma-aṅgas, and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, the guardians of the image (*mūrtipāḥ*) should also perform oblations with a tenth part of the number of oblations performed by the preceptor. Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, [he offers] sacrificial wood, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*),
parched grain (*lāja*), mung beans, black gram, barley, sesame, rice, wheat, wild rice (*nīvāra*), flour, white mustard, and curd.
Māṣa-cakes, jaggery-cakes, milk-rice, and fruits and the like;
as well as cardamom, cloves, camphor, musk, and saffron.
One should offer gorojana, musk, and betel-leaf in sequence;

One should offer wild rice with the Śikhā-mantra, groats with the Kavaca-mantra, and white mustard seeds with the Pāśupata-mantra, while reciting the Puruṣa-mantra. (5) One should perform the oblation with a focused mind.
One should offer oblations, one by one in sequence, of black gram cakes, molasses cakes, milk-rice, fruits, and so forth, along with the weapon-mantra (astramantra). (I.66a)

(3) For each of the thirty-eight substances, an oblation is prescribed; for each of those substances to be offered, one should sacrifice with the *vyāhṛtis*. (4)

The Daṇḍabhaṅginī-nyāsa: *Oṃ hoṃ*, salutation to Īśāna, the head; *Oṃ he*, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the face; *Oṃ huṃ*, salutation to Aghora, the heart; *Oṃ hiṃ*, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret organ; *Oṃ haṃ*, salutation to Sadyojāta, the form. Having thus performed the placement (*vinyasya*), [follows] the Muṇḍabhaṅginī-nyāsa: *Oṃ hoṃ*, salutation to Īśāna, the head... [and so forth].

(i.66b) One should worship by meditating thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, the form of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, to Śiva. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sannidhāna*), and firm fixation (*sannirodhana*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*), one should adorn [the deity] with perfumes, garlands of flowers, and so forth. Having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) using that mantra, one should display the *sṛk* mudrā. Then, having offered incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and the like, one should effect the union of the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of the fire.

(4) Having offered a hundred oblations with its root mantra for the purpose of satisfying the mantra, and having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); and having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of special satisfaction, and having given the full oblation; (5) for the sake of bringing about the [proper] place and time, pacifying ill omens, and bringing about auspicious omens, having offered a hundred oblations each with the root mantra, and having given the full oblation; [one performs] the satisfaction with: *oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā*.

One should perform the kindling (*dīpana*) with three oblations [reciting]: *oṃ hūṃ haṃ hūṃ sadyojātāya huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having offered one hundred oblations of *aśvattha* wood with the mantra *oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā*, and having given the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should offer the sacrificial substances such as *śimbā* and others, either in the previously mentioned number or according to one's capacity, [with the following mantras]: *oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ vāyave svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ sūryāya svāhā*; *oṃ hāṃ prajāpataye svāhā*.

Thus, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances, (5) having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, having offered the *caru* preceded by the Guru, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*), betel, and so forth, and having performed the recitation (*japa*), the offering (*nivedya*), and the prostration (6)—thus concludes the procedure for the western fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
